explanations.explanation: That's exactly what they say. The lords rejoice and say, "Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands." They are praising Dagon, their god, for putting Samson in their hands. I think the whole room felt like they'd won the big game.

explanations.answer: Sent rain down on their fields
explanations.explanation: Nope, rain isn't what they say their god did. The lords gather to offer a great sacrifice to Dagon, and they say, "Our god has delivered Samson our enemy into our hands." Their celebration is about Samson, friend.

Good guess for a party, but this one's not about crops. The lords gather for a great sacrifice to Dagon and say their god has delivered Samson into their hands. Their cheering is all about catching one man. The harvest never comes up.

Yes, that's what the people say when they see him. They praise their god for delivering "…our enemy who destroyed our land and multiplied our dead." Those are their words about Samson, and they're loud about it. I think a crowd that's been holding that in for a while finally gets to let it out.

This one is true. When the people see Samson, they praise their god and say he is the enemy "…who destroyed our land and multiplied our dead." That's the text, word for word. It's a lot to say about one man in a prison, but they said it.
Right, the word is entertain. They say, "Call for Samson to entertain us." So out of the prison he comes. I think a crowd with merry hearts wanted a show, and he was who they asked for.
Close, but that's not the word they use. The Philistines say, "Call for Samson to entertain us." The word is entertain, and they say it while their hearts are merry.

That's a fun word to land on, since Samson judged Israel for twenty years (Judges 16:31). But here the crowd isn't asking for a judge. They say, "Call for Samson to entertain us." The word is entertain.
That's the one. The text says, "And they stationed him between the pillars." Remember that word, because those pillars are about to matter a lot.
Gates make sense for a city, but this is the temple. The text says they stationed Samson "…between the pillars." Gates just aren't part of this scene.
The party started with a sacrifice to Dagon, so altars would fit the mood. But the text says they stationed him "…between the pillars." Keep an eye on those pillars, friend.

Right. Samson tells the servant, "Lead me where I can feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them." The servant is holding his hand, so he's being led. I bet it sounded like an ordinary request to the servant.
Not quite. Samson asks to be led where he can "…feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them." He wants to touch them and lean on them. Hiding isn't in his words.

Good thinking, but the crowd doesn't come up in what he asks. He says, "Lead me where I can feel the pillars supporting the temple, so I can lean against them." The reason he gives is to lean on the pillars.
Yes. Samson prays, "Strengthen me, O God, just once more…" He asks God directly, and he asks for it one time. Notice he starts with "…please remember me." so he comes to God first.
This one is true. Samson prays, "O Lord GOD, please remember me. Strengthen me, O God, just once more…" He asks for strength, and he asks for it one more time. It's right there in his prayer.

That's what he prays. He asks that "…with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes." He says it plainly to the LORD. I think this is a heavy moment, so I'll just say it's what he asked.

explanations.answer: Break him free of his shackles
explanations.explanation: His prayer isn't about shackles. He asks for strength so that "…with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes." The blow is for paying back the Philistines, and shackles never come up in his prayer.

explanations.answer: Win him a way back home
explanations.explanation: Not what he asks. Samson prays that "…with one vengeful blow I may pay back the Philistines for my two eyes." There's no mention of home in his prayer. His family does come for him and bury him later (Judges 16:31).

explanations.answer: Let me die with the Philistines
explanations.explanation: Yes, those are his words. With his right hand on one pillar and his left on the other, Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines." I think this is the heaviest line in the passage, so we'll let it stand as it is.

explanations.answer: Let me go free from this place
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says. Standing braced between the pillars, Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines." He doesn't ask to go free. It's a hard thing to hear.

explanations.answer: Let me rest here for a while
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says. He braces himself against the two pillars and says, "Let me die with the Philistines." Resting isn't in his words. It's a heavy line.

explanations.answer: It falls on the lords and all the people
explanations.explanation: That's right. Samson pushes "…with all his might, and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it." The two pillars he had his hands on were holding it up. One more thing to notice: it's a heavy ending to the scene.

The temple doesn't just shake. The text says Samson "…pushed with all his might, and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it." It comes down. Earlier he had asked the LORD to strengthen him just once more.

explanations.answer: Only the roof comes crashing down
explanations.explanation: The text says more than that. Samson pushed with all his might, "…and the temple fell on the lords and all the people in it." The whole temple falls, not just the roof. Remember, there were about three thousand people up on that roof (Judges 16:27).
It's the other way around. The text says, "So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life." That's a big statement, given everything Samson had done before this. More, not fewer.
Yes, this one is false. The text says, "So in his death he killed more than he had killed in his life." More in that one moment than all the years before it. That's what the writer tells us.

Yes. His brothers and his father's family carried him back and buried him "…between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah." His family came for him. I think that's a quiet, kind ending to a loud story.
Machpelah is a real burial place, where Abraham buried Sarah (Genesis 23:19). But it's not where Samson goes. His family buries him "…between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah."

The text says otherwise. Samson's brothers and his father's family "…came down, carried him back…" and buried him between Zorah and Eshtaol in the tomb of his father Manoah. Gaza isn't the burial place the text names.
